events.title: PHP 7.0 released
events.summary: The PHP project released PHP 7.0 on December 3, 2015 — roughly doubling performance and adding scalar type hints and the spaceship operator.
events.about: PHP 7 revived the language after years on PHP 5: WordPress, Laravel, and Symfony sites ran dramatically faster on the same hardware. Scalar types and return declarations brought optional static discipline without losing PHP's deploy-by-FTP simplicity.

narrative.whyChosen: PHP 7 was the performance reboot that kept PHP relevant against Node and Python.
narrative.whyImportant: A 2× speedup on real workloads changed hosting economics for millions of sites.
narrative.problemSolved: PHP 5.6 was slow and aging; the ecosystem needed a breaking cleanup to modernize internals.

events.title: Swift open-sourced
events.summary: Apple open-sourced Swift on December 3, 2015 under the Apache 2.0 license — releasing the compiler, standard library, and Swift.org governance model.
events.about: Open Swift let the language run on Linux servers, attracted outside contributors, and separated Swift from pure Apple platform lock-in. It enabled server-side Swift experiments and laid groundwork for Swift on Windows and cross-platform tooling.

narrative.whyChosen: Open-sourcing Swift was Apple's bid to make it a general-purpose language, not just an iOS detail.
narrative.whyImportant: Community governance and Linux support expanded where Swift could run.
narrative.problemSolved: Swift was tied to Xcode; server and open-source adopters needed a portable toolchain.

events.title: Perl 6.0.0 'Christmas' released
events.summary: The Perl 6 team shipped version 6.c 'Christmas' on December 25, 2015 — the first production-ready Perl 6 after 15 years of design.
events.about: Perl 6 (later renamed Raku) brought grammars, gradual typing, and concurrency primitives to the Perl family. The Christmas release marked the end of 'Perl 6 is coming' jokes and gave the community a compiler (Rakudo) to build on.

narrative.whyChosen: After a decade and a half, Perl 6 finally shipped as a real language.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved long-running language redesigns could reach production, even if adoption stayed niche.
narrative.problemSolved: Perl 5 could not evolve radically without breaking its massive installed base.
